Mapping with a walking robot is really tough compared to wheeled robots. The odometry is noisy, the Lidar shakes with every step, and the drift can ruin a map in seconds."
""
"To get this result using ROS 2 Humble, I had to dig deep into the control architecture:"
""
"The Engineering Fixes:"
""
"• Hardware Calibration: Wrote a custom Python script to mechanically trim every servo to the exact pulse width, fixing a 20-degree assembly error in the front-left hip."
""
"• Gait Synchronization: Developed a threaded teleop node to lock the walking speed to exactly 0.06 m/s—the sweet spot where the Lidar frequency matches the gait cycle."
""
"• Sensor Fusion: Tuned the EKF (Extended Kalman Filter) to fuse RF2O (Laser Odometry) with IMU data, stabilizing the map even when the robot slips."
""
"The result? Sharp walls, perfect loop closures, and a robot that finally knows where it is."
""
"Again thank you Scientist G for this amazing opportunity."

Remote Teleoperation and System Integration on PuppyPi via ROS 2."
""
"Hello World is standard, but Hello Walk is where the real engineering begins."
"We’ve reached a major milestone with our quadruped project: Full Remote Teleoperation is live. While the hardware came with standard demos, we wanted a robust, developer-friendly architecture that allows us to control and debug the robot from anywhere."
""
"Here is the custom ROS 2 Humble stack we built to make it happen:"
""
"1. The Nervous System (Tailscale & SSH) Real robots don't always stay on the local network. We integrated Tailscale to create a secure, mesh VPN. This allows us to SSH into the Pi and stream high-bandwidth data (Lidar/Video) seamlessly, treating the remote robot as if it were right next to us."
""
"2. The Eyes (Foxglove Studio) Debugging blind is a nightmare. We set up the Foxglove Bridge to visualize the robot's perception in real-time. Seeing the TF tree, camera stream, and Lidar scan (LD19) overlay instantly on a web dashboard has drastically speeded up our testing cycle."
""
"3. The Brain (Custom Launch Architecture) We moved away from scattered scripts and built a custom overlay package (my_puppy). A single master launch file now orchestrates the entire startup sequence:"
""
"Body: Initializing the ros_robot_controller for servo/IMU communication."
"Kinematics: Launching the gait engine."
"Sensors: Bringing up the Lidar and optimized Camera nodes."
""
"4. Control (SSH Teleop) Standard teleop nodes weren't cutting it for the specific gait logic of this quadruped. We wrote a custom Python-based keyboard controller to manage state transitions (Sit/Stand/Walk) and send precise velocity commands directly to the navigation stack."
""
"And we used VDO ninja to stream the overview camera that is a mobile phone camera to see what the actual robot is doing. "
""
"Status & Next Steps: The robot is standing up and taking its first remote-controlled steps. We are currently fine-tuning the gait synchronization to smooth out the movement and eliminate micro-stutters, ensuring the walk is as fluid as the architecture behind it."
"As well as freezing the camera frames issue."
""
"Next up: Sensor Fusion & SLAM. Time to make a map, ofcourse after the fine tuning and calibration. "
""

Squeezing Every Drop of Performance from the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano"
""
"Optimization isn't just about speed—it's about efficiency."
""
"We benchmarked the Ultra-Fast Lane Detection (UFLD) model running on ROS 2 & Python to see just how much compute we could save on the Edge. By migrating from PyTorch to TensorRT, the results were staggering."
""
"The Benchmark Results (Capped at 30 FPS):"
""
"🔴 PyTorch (FP16) Latency: ~28 ms | GPU Load: ~60% Verdict: Heavy compute load but better than PyTorch (FP32) [~20% more heavier]"
""
"🟡 TensorRT (FP32) Latency: ~23 ms | GPU Load: ~40% Verdict: Improved, but still resource-intensive."
""
"🟢 TensorRT (FP16) — The Sweet Spot Latency: ~19 ms | GPU Load: ~20% Verdict: Ideally balanced speed and efficiency."
""
"🚀 TensorRT (INT8) — Max Velocity Latency: ~17 ms | GPU Load: ~10% Verdict: Maximum speed, minimal load."
""
"Key Insights: "
"🔹 Resource Liberation: Switching to TensorRT FP16 dropped GPU usage by 3x, leaving 80% of the GPU free for processes like Lidar, SLAM, and Path Planning. "
"🔹 The Accuracy Trade-off: While INT8 is the efficiency king (only 10% load!), we observed a visual drop in lane tracking accuracy compared to FP16. "
"🔹 Edge Mode: All metrics were pulled off using jetson_clocks, simulating maximum performance mode for deployment."
""
"And this is just with Python. Converting this pipeline to C++ or NVIDIA Isaac ROS could unlock even lower latencies and zero-copy transfer speeds."
""

Beyond the final rank, the real trophy from BAJA SAEINDIA is the deep engineering experience. For my network of developers and roboticists, I wanted to share the core technical architecture that our team, Team Equinox, built to bring our autonomous vehicle to life."
""
"My role was leading the Autonomous Systems Integration, the incredible challenge of bridging the high-level world of ROS 2 with the low-level reality of our vehicle's hardware. This was a journey in making two different worlds speak the same language."
""
"Our entire system was architected around a central NVIDIA Jetson by Tanna TechBiz LLP running ROS 2 and connected to a Kvaser AB dual channel CAN adapter to interface it directly to the CAN network communicating with five distributed Arduino UNO R4 Minima microcontrollers over a robust CAN bus network. Each Arduino served as a dedicated, real-time "muscle controller" for a specific task (Startup, Dashboard, Throttle, Brakes, Steering)."
""
"This was a true team effort, and I was the fortunate integrator connecting the brilliant work of two major sub-teams:"
""
"First, the low-level Electrical Team, led by Naveen Shaji George and Muhammed Ajmal K with their incredible crew. They were the masters of the physical layer, designing the PCBs, building the complex wiring harness, and patiently debugging every circuit with me. Their work was the foundation everything was built on. When a relay fired unexpectedly or a sensor gave a noisy reading, they were the ones who found the solution in the hardware."
""
"Second, the high-level Autonomous Software Team, led by ASHISH SHAJAN and Tomin Michael. They were the masters of the "brain," developing the perception and control algorithms in ROS 2. They gave me the high-level commands—the "what to do.""
""
"My job was to build the "how." This involved architecting the CAN protocol, writing the firmware for the Arduino nodes, and developing the central C++ ROS 2 can_interface node that acted as the real-time translator between the two worlds. The challenge was immense, from solving CAN bus arbitration conflicts to tuning PD controllers for our actuators and designing safety-critical state machines to pass the rigorous Technical Inspections."
""
"The interface node includes converting the Starkenn Technologies Radar encoded CAN data to ROS messages through the DBC file. "
""
"This experience was a profound lesson in how crucial the role of a systems integrator is. It's about understanding both the hardware and software worlds deeply enough to make them work together seamlessly. A massive thank you to both teams and many others who worked behind the scenes, for their collaboration, patience, and expertise. We built this together. "

"🔹 High-Fidelity URDF: A detailed XACRO-based robot model, including a kinematically correct pan-tilt mechanism and properly defined sensor frames (REP-103 compliant) for the HP60C RGB-D camera and IMU."

Five days. That's the time our team had to learn MATLAB & Simulink and deliver a solution for the MathWorks Minidrone Competition while we were going through our exams. We started with the excellent framework provided by MathWorks—including the drone model and physics simulation—and our task was to engineer the brain."
""
"This is the result: a complete autonomous navigation and landing algorithm."
""
"Our design is a hybrid state machine that intelligently switches between two control modes to maximize stability and precision:"
""
"1. High-Level Position Control (pos_ref):"
"For stable flight phases like following a straight line, we command the drone with waypoints in the fixed world coordinate system. A P-controller uses visual feedback to calculate the sideways (Y) component of the waypoint, while a discrete integrator calculates the forward (X) component, resulting in smooth, continuous motion."
""
"2. Low-Level Attitude Control (orient_ref):"
"For sharp, on-the-spot turns, position control is too sluggish. We switch to attitude control to command a precise Yaw Angle. This gives us direct control over the drone's heading, allowing for crisp, predictable 90-degree turns."
""
"The Vision System:"
"To feed the state machine, we built a multi-ROI vision pipeline. A "look-ahead" region of the camera feed analyzes the path's Orientation to detect upcoming turns, while a "steering" region analyzes the Centroid to provide real-time feedback for our line-following P-controller."
""
"The Brutally Honest Part:"
"This controller is a specialist. It's tuned and architected for tracks with cardinal (90-degree) turns."
""
" Why won't it work on a 45-degree turn? Because our straight-line logic explicitly separates "forward" and "sideways" into the world X and Y axes. After a 90-degree turn, we can simply swap these roles. But for a 45-degree turn, "forward" becomes a mix of X and Y, and this simple logic breaks down. A truly universal controller would require a more complex, drone-centric (trigonometric) navigation model."
""
"This project was an incredible deep dive into the realities of control systems."
""

The spec sheet for a device like the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano only tells half the story. To see what it's really capable of, We ran a series of CPU benchmarks across its different power profiles. We wanted to see the real numbers behind the marketing, and the results are telling."

"The method was straightforward: use nvpmodel to select a power profile, jetson_clocks to lock the frequencies for that mode, and sysbench to run a 6-thread prime number calculation. Live stats were monitored with jtop."

"Here's a direct comparison of the three key modes:"

"25W Mode: This is the default high-performance profile. It locks the CPU at 1.34 GHz and gives the GPU maximum priority. This scored 3448 events per second."
"(Which is really interesting cause its supposed to be at 1.7GHz as I tested and confirmed with another Orin nano before. "

""
"15W Mode: Interestingly, this lower power mode produced a higher CPU score of 3843 events per second. The jetson_clocks output shows why: it allocates less power to the GPU, allowing the CPU to lock in at a faster 1.5 GHz."
"(Which is expected ofc)"
""
"MAXN_SUPER Mode: This is the unconstrained, "max-effort" mode. It removes the official wattage limit entirely. The result was a big performance increase, scoring 4437 events per second."
"The most important finding came from running jtop in MAXN mode. The Orin Nano CPU pushed past its official 1.5 GHz specification, holding a completely stable 1.7 GHz on all six cores under full load. Total system power draw was a modest 11.1W for this CPU-only test, and the CPU temperature stayed at a healthy 71C. Plus the GPU was 1.02Ghz which is the max we found out."

The results are in, and they're not subtle. Here's a side-by-side look at why a simple Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) is not enough for robust SLAM, and how an EKF changes everything."
""
"For our autonomous UGV,  we put two SLAM architectures to a head-to-head test in a challenging indoor simulation. The mission: create a clean, globally consistent map(A small single room)."
""
"Top Video: System A (VIO-Only SLAM)"
""
"This is what happens when you rely solely on a visual-inertial source for odometry. Watch closely:"
"🔹 Fragility: Notice how easily the system gets lost (the dreaded "red screen" in rtabmap-viz) during turns or fast movements."
"🔹 Map Fragmentation: Each time the VIO fails, our Odom/ResetCountdown feature correctly kicks in to recover, but this creates disconnected "map islands.""
"🔹 Failed Loop Closures: At the end, when the robot returns to the start, the accumulated drift between the islands is so massive that the system correctly rejects the loop closures to avoid corrupting the map entirely."
"🔹 The Result: A distorted, fragmented, and unusable map."
""
"Bottom Video: System B (EKF-Fused SLAM)"
""
"This is the exact same task, but with one critical difference: we've added a robot_localization Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to fuse the fragile VIO with the simulation's stable (but drifty) wheel odometry and IMU. The difference is night and day:"
"🔸 Robustness: The EKF acts as a "shock absorber." When the VIO fails, the EKF seamlessly "coasts" on the other sensors, providing a continuous odometry stream. The map never stops growing."
"🔸 No Islands: Because the EKF's output is continuous, the SLAM node sees no reason to create new map islands. The map is built as a single, cohesive entity."
"🔸 Successful Loop Closure: The EKF's filtering dramatically reduces odometry drift. When the robot returns to the start, the loop closure is mathematically sound and is ACCEPTED (is what I would like to say but as this is a simulation and the environment is bland amd feature less, therefore the final loop closure didnt happen, even still we got a pretty good map)."
"🔸 The Result: A clean, geometrically correct, and globally consistent map, ready for navigation."
""
"The Conclusion:"
"Our experiment confirms what the official RTAB-Map research paper states: for robust navigation, fusing with other sensors like wheel odometry and IMU is mandatory. The EKF isn't just a "nice to have"; it is the foundational component that provides the fault tolerance necessary for real-world autonomy."
""
"While a simulation is always more visually sparse than reality (leading to fewer loop closures than we'd expect on our UGV), the difference in architectural robustness is undeniable."

"Every great machine learning model is built on a foundation of great data. But in the real world, data is rarely clean, consistent, or balanced. I'm excited to share a project I developed to tackle this challenge head-on: a YOLO Dataset Toolkit."

"This toolkit is a set of Python scripts designed to take on the "janitorial" work of data preparation, turning multiple, messy sources into a high-quality, training-ready dataset."
""
"The Journey from Raw Data to a Perfect Training Set:"
""
"    The Challenge: We started by sourcing data from multiple public projects. Each came with its own structure, class names (stop vs. Red Light), and quality."
""
"    The Problem: Simply combining these sources resulted in a severely imbalanced dataset, with some classes having 10x more images than others—a recipe for a biased model."
""
"    The Solution: I built a configurable Python script that unifies the datasets. It uses a mapping file to standardize all class names and consolidate the data into a single, clean format."
""
"    The Result: A perfectly balanced dataset, created by automatically under-sampling the majority classes. We went from a chaotic mix to a perfectly structured set, ready for training."
""
"    The Extra Mile: To ensure quality, I even added an interactive OpenCV-based tool to let a human reviewer quickly spot-check images and flag any mislabeled data."
""
"This project was a deep dive into the practical side of MLOps and data engineering. Building a solid data pipeline is a critical first step before any model training can begin, and I'm proud of the robust and reusable toolkit that came out of it."
""

""
"Thrilled to share my first successful project using micro-ROS! Building on my recent journey into the ESP-IDF framework [(https://lnkd.in/g55Bzgc8)], "
"I wanted to bridge the gap between embedded systems and the broader ROS 2 ecosystem."
""
"The Goal: Create a simple teleoperation system. Press WASD/Space on my ROS 2 Humble (Ubuntu 22) host machine, send a command to an ESP32 running micro-ROS, and have the ESP32 report its state back to the host."
""
"The Journey & Learnings:"
""
"    Environment: Leveraged the official microros/esp-idf-microros Docker container – a huge time-saver for managing the complex ESP-IDF toolchain and micro-ROS dependencies!"
""
"    Architecture: The system uses the standard micro-ROS Client/Agent architecture. The ESP32 runs the micro-ROS client, communicating via UDP over WiFi with the micro-ROS Agent running on my laptop, which bridges messages to/from the main ROS 2 network (DDS)."
""
"    Debugging Challenges: The path wasn't straight!"
""
"        Encountered initial C compilation errors on the ESP32 when trying to use std_msgs/msg/String directly for publishing status. This highlighted tricky aspects of memory management and type handling with rclc string functions in this environment."
""
"        The Workaround: Pivoted to using simple std_msgs/msg/Int32 for the core communication. WASD/Space keys are mapped to integers (1-4, 0) on the host, sent to the ESP32, which then publishes back the received integer status. A separate host node translates this integer back to user-friendly text ("MOVING FORWARD", "STOPPED", etc.). This proved much more robust on the embedded side."
""
"        Debugged intermittent rcl_publish failures (RCL_RET_ERROR, handled by RCSOFTCHECK) on the ESP32, confirming they were related to UDP packet loss over my WiFi network – a good reminder of real-world network considerations!"
""
"    Persistence Pays Off at last."
""
"The Result:"
""
"It works! As shown in the attached video demo, I have three host terminals:"
""
"    The micro-ROS Agent bridging communication."
""
"    My Python keyboard node (wasd_teleop) publishing integer commands (1-4, 0) to /wasd_command."
""
"    My Python status display node (status_display) subscribing to /wasd_status from the ESP32 and printing the corresponding action ("MOVING FORWARD", "STOPPED", etc.)."
""
"This project was a fantastic hands-on introduction to micro-ROS concepts like publishers, subscribers, executors, the agent's role, and debugging across distributed ROS 2 systems. Really excited to apply this to more complex robotics projects integrating sensors and actuators on microcontrollers!"
